chunks.text: There is also one page of Reading for Pleasure , which is related to the Reading for Pleasure material in the Coursebook. There are two Review and Reference pages at the end of each theme which provide revision activities for the grammar introduced in that theme, as well as a vocabulary activity based on the words and phrases in the Glossary at the end of each theme in the Coursebook. The end material of the Workbook in Grade 12B consists of: • a Reading Section with comprehension questions for timed reading practice • Communication Activities • Writing Activities • Grammar Practice Activities • a Writing Guide Section for each theme • a Grammar Reference Section for each theme • a Word List for each theme • a Functional Language Review for each theme • Answers to the Across Cultures and Review and Reference activities. The Grammar Practice activities are a new feature of the Grade 11 and 12 Workbooks, and provide students with further opportunities to practise the grammar presented in Unit 2 of each theme. 1.3.3 The T eacher’s Book The T eacher’s Book provides an introduction to the curriculum for Grades 11 and 12, an outline of the course components and detailed suggestions about how to use the course materials. Listening scripts are provided in the teaching notes. 1.3.4 Course CD All recordings used during the course are included on a CD supplied with the other course components. 2. Course Materials 2.1 The Coursebook The Coursebook opens with a Contents Map, which outlines the syllabus. This is followed by a two-page spread with the learning objectives for each theme, for students’ easy reference. 2.1.1 Overview page The overview page for each theme is intended to introduce the topic, and activate students’ prior knowledge about the subject. Students are usually asked to look at a number of photographs or pictures and discuss their content and/or some questions associated with the general theme. There is also a short text that introduces the sub-themes and which contains relevant vocabulary. A number of words and phrases are presented in bold lettering, all of which will occur in the theme. These words can be used for spelling practice, in addition to the 12 – 14 words presented in the Glossary in the Review and Reference section at the end of each theme in the Coursebook. 2.1.2 Reading The focus of Unit 1 in each theme is reading. Students read a variety of reading texts using a range of strategies and reading skills. The materials in this unit focus on different reading micro-skills, such as ‘recognising topic sentences’ or ‘inferring information’. Realistic purposes for reading are developed with naturalistic texts being used in a variety of text types. Both informational reading and reading for

chunks.title: دليل المعلم مادة اللغة الإنجليزية teachers book للصف الثاني عشر الفصل الثاني
chunks.text: The materials in this unit focus on different reading micro-skills, such as ‘recognising topic sentences’ or ‘inferring information’. Realistic purposes for reading are developed with naturalistic texts being used in a variety of text types. Both informational reading and reading for xv • Teacher’s Book • Introduction pleasure are developed with a focus on both intensive and extensive reading. The final activity in each unit is a discussion activity, Time to T alk , which picks up on a topic associated with the content of a reading text. This gives students the opportunity to express their ideas and opinions in small discussion groups, and then present the results of their discussion to the rest of the class. As mentioned in 1.3.1, the ideas generated by each Time to T alk activity are used as the basis for extra writing practice. Students are asked to write a paragraph, details of which are given in each theme. Suggestions and guidelines for paragraph structure are given in the T eacher’s Book. 2.1.3 Grammar The focus of Unit 2 in each theme is grammar . This unit provides the opportunity to review and consolidate specific areas of grammar which have been encountered earlier in the English for Me course. The grammar items are presented in clear contexts with a balance of inductive and deductive tasks. The practical function of grammar is demonstrated through an equal emphasis on meaning and form. The grammar tasks are discussed and analysed orally, and this is followed up by a pair/group speaking activity Activate your English . This activity focuses on the accurate oral production of the grammar items being revised, through creating a dialogue. 2.1.4 Vocabulary The focus of Unit 3 in each theme is vocabulary development. In addition to the acquisition of vocabulary through a wide variety of reading and listening texts, there is a focus on the teaching of high-frequency vocabulary used in different contexts. Opportunities are created to help students make their receptive vocabulary productive through the process of recycling. Students are exposed to word-building activities which involve them in working out how words are put together and how to work out the meaning of unknown vocabulary from context. There is a wide variety of activities to maintain students’ interest in vocabulary development, such as crosswords. 2.1.5 Listening and Speaking Unit 4 of each theme focuses on oral skills. It aims to develop fluency and accuracy within specified functional areas and with acceptable standards of pronunciation.There is a focus throughout on developing realistic purposes for listening, including both listening for pleasure and listening for information.

chunks.title: دليل المعلم مادة اللغة الإنجليزية teachers book للصف الثاني عشر الفصل الثاني
chunks.text: 2.1.5 Listening and Speaking Unit 4 of each theme focuses on oral skills. It aims to develop fluency and accuracy within specified functional areas and with acceptable standards of pronunciation.There is a focus throughout on developing realistic purposes for listening, including both listening for pleasure and listening for information. The listening tasks can be dialogues between two or more speakers, or just one speaker talking about a topic. They simulate interviews, radio shows and short presentations. In each unit there is a Soundbites activity which highlights the functional language highlighted in the unit, such as asking for clarification on complaining and responding to complaints. This both revises and extends previous work covered, providing more options for students to use in conversation. Soundbites is followed by an activity where the focus is on the fluent use of the functional language highlighted in the Soundbites box. 2.1.6 Writing The emphasis in Unit 5 is on developing purposeful and practical writing skills, rather than writing for its own sake or in order to practise grammatical structures. A wide variety of writing tasks is given, but teachers should also look for opportunities to create more, for example, writing tasks based on a discussion. Each of the writing units in the four themes in the new Grade 12 books leads up to a main task in one of four writing genres – narrative, interactive, evaluative and informative. Students are taken through the various stages of reading a model text, then analysing its language and features to help them build up a first draft of an essay. They work on editing and improving their first draft, often with the help of a partner , before producing a final draft. 2.1.7 Across Cultures and Reading for Pleasure These are optional two-page spreads which teachers can choose either to do in class with students or ask students to complete in their own xvi • Teacher’s Book • Introduction time. There are no detailed activity notes in the T eacher’s Book. Each of the Across Cultures spreads focuses on a different country, particularly on aspects of interest to Omani students who might be going to study in that country. At the end of each spread, students discuss questions which compare an aspect of the culture they have read about with Oman - for example, sports or food. They discuss the questions and then write a paragraph giving particular information about Oman to a visitor , based on the ideas generated in their discussions. The Reading for Pleasure spread introduces a range of text types and genres, which it is hoped that students will enjoy. Interested students can find additional information about the topic on the Reading for Pleasure page in the Workbook.

Although there are no specific activities for Reading for Pleasure , teachers might like to ask students to do a short piece of writing – for example, a short summary, or to say whether they found what they read interesting, and give their reasons. 2.1.8 Review and Reference Page The Review and Reference page outlines the main learning activities/objectives the students have covered in the theme. In addition, there is a Glossary containing 12 – 14 of the core words. T eachers should tell students to learn the spellings of the words in the Glossary, and check these spellings at the end of the theme. 2.1.9 Communication Activities Several of the themes generate communication activities which require students to turn to specific pages in the back of the book. All materials for these activities are fully cross-referenced. 2.2 The Workbook The Workbook opens with a Contents Map, which outlines the syllabus. This is followed by a two-page spread with the learning outcomes for each theme. 2.2.1 Reading The two-page reading spread provides practice activities for a reading text from the Coursebook or a second reading text, plus further practice of the activity type related to the text. In addition, there may be vocabulary activities linked to the topic of the unit or activities which require students to complete an activity with personal information. 2.2.2 Grammar The grammar pages provide further consolidation and practice activities related to the language focus areas of the unit. Students also work on vocabulary activities. 2.2.3 Vocabulary The vocabulary pages provide opportunities for students to use the vocabulary introduced in the listening or reading texts. Students also complete word-building and vocabulary extension activities. 2.2.4 Listening and Speaking The listening and speaking pages give students the opportunity to complete their answers to listening activities, and to work on the functional language contained in the Soundbites box in the Coursebook. 2.2.5 Writing The writing pages give students practice with a variety of tasks related to the writing genre focused on in the theme. The activities aim to build up to the writing task which is the main output of the theme such as writing an essay or a letter .

The activities aim to build up to the writing task which is the main output of the theme such as writing an essay or a letter . 2.2.6 Across Cultures and Reading for Pleasure The Across Cultures page provides activities linked to the Across Cultures spread in the Coursebook. The activities can be worked on in class or by individual students in their own time. In response to requests from teachers, answer keys to the Across Cultures activities have been provided in the T eacher’s Book at the end of each theme, as well as in the Workbook. The Reading for Pleasure page is related to the topic of the Reading for Pleasure two-page spread in the Coursebook. It provides areas for further xvii • Teacher’s Book • discussion, or for students to think about. 2.2.7 Review and Reference Pages The Review and Reference pages at the end of each theme contain a self-assessment activity and practice activities for grammar and vocabulary revised in the theme. In response to requests from teachers, answer keys for the Review and Reference activities have been provided in the T eacher’s Book at the end of each theme, as well as at the back of the Workbook. In addition, students personalise their learning by choosing 18 words from the theme that they would like to remember – 6 nouns, 6 verbs and 6 adjectives. The last activity of the Review and Reference section is a Personalise It activity, in which students choose two things that interest them, two things new to them and two things from each theme that they wish to find out more about. 2.2.8 Communication Activities There are a number of communication activities which require students to turn to specific pages in the back of the book. All materials for these activities are fully cross-referenced. 2.2.9 Writing Activities In the Grade 12B Workbook, there are Writing Activity pages where students write their own CV and complete a job application form. 2.2.10 Grammar Practice The Grammar Practice pages are a new feature of the Grade 11 and 12 books. There are four Grammar Practice activity pages – one for each theme. They provide the opportunity for further practice of the main grammar point focused on in the theme, plus other points. 2.2.11 Writing Guide The Writing Guide section focuses on the main writing task for that theme. Guidance is given concerning layout and language, and models provided for students to follow.

It is intended to provide a reminder and further support for those students who may need more help. 2.2.13 Word List This is arranged by theme, and comprises the key vocabulary presented in the Glossary at the end of each theme in the Coursebook. There is a phonetic transcription for each word. 2.2.14 Functional Language Review This contains the phrases from the Soundbites function boxes presented in each theme of the Coursebook, set out on one page for students’ easy reference. 2.3 The T eacher’s Book 2.3.1 Contents Map and Learning Objectives A Contents Map is provided at the front of the T eacher’s Book which outlines the syllabus. This is followed by a two-page spread with the learning objectives for each theme. It should be noted that these objectives are not exhaustive and may not represent each separate activity. The learning objectives are followed by cross-curricular links which relate the material presented in the course to other areas of the school curriculum. 2.3.2 Approach The teacher’s notes are written in units, rather than lessons. Although no specific timings for activities have been given, it is expected that, with the reduction of the Grade 11 and 12 books from five themes to four , teachers will be able to cover most of the material. However , it is also recognised that some classes may work faster and others may progress at a slower rate if students have difficulty with a particular language point or skill. It is therefore up to individual teachers to allocate the time they spend on individual activities, according to the ability of their class. Summary of Activities In response to requests from teachers, there is more freedom for teachers to work through the Introduction xviii • Teacher’s Book • Introduction course materials. T o help teachers, on the introductory page to each theme, a summary is given so that teachers can see at a glance the activities which the theme contains. It is therefore essential for teachers to read through each theme thoroughly before they start it in class, to familiarise themselves with the activities. The activities are laid out in a suggested order , alternating between Coursebook and Workbook, but it is up to individual teachers to decide if they want to follow that order . Some themes contain additional activities.

chunks.text: It is therefore essential for teachers to read through each theme thoroughly before they start it in class, to familiarise themselves with the activities. The activities are laid out in a suggested order , alternating between Coursebook and Workbook, but it is up to individual teachers to decide if they want to follow that order . Some themes contain additional activities. Again, it is up to individual teachers to decide whether they wish to make use of these extra activities, and if so, whether to do them in class or give them as homework. Pair/Group work Pair and group work are included throughout the course. These activities are intended to give students more practice in oral skills. With many activities, it is up to the teacher to decide if they should be done only orally, or whether students should also write the answers in their exercise books. In addition, there are many discussion activities throughout each theme to give students the chance to work together and engage with the content of a unit. T eachers should use these activities as an opportunity to monitor and assess students continuously and informally. Feedback and Monitoring Within the detailed teaching notes there is often only a brief mention made to obtaining class feedback in the interests of space and constant repetition. However , there are a number of ways in which feedback can be given. Simple checking of answers can be teacher-led by choosing individual students to answer . Feedback from group discussions can be done in a number of ways: • The discussion can be opened up so that the whole class gets a chance to participate. • A spokesperson from each group can be asked to provide feedback from their group. Once all the groups have spoken, then the discussion can be refocused to pick up on points arising from the discussion. • One group can lead the feedback, facilitating the discussion in place of the teacher . This gives students valuable practice in facilitation skills which is useful in many career areas. • T wo groups can work together and summarise to each other the points arising from their discussions. T eachers are advised to use the opportunities provided by the more independent learning activities to monitor and assess students’ oral skills while they work in groups, or their written work throughout the drafting and checking process. 2.3.3 T eaching Notes Detailed teaching notes are provided for each unit outlining what students are required to do in each activity. Listening scripts are provided in the detailed teaching notes. 2.3.4 Course CDs The course CDs feature a variety of native speakers of English as well as Omani voices.

chunks.text: 2 Theme 1 Unit 1 Press Photography • Teacher’s Book • Lead-in Direct students to the title of the theme. Ask them what they understand by ‘the media. ’ The media: A collective word meaning organisations that provide news and information, such as newspapers, magazines, TV and radio stations. ‘Media’ can also be used as an adjective, e.g. A job in media research . Ask students some general questions about news, such as: • Do you think that news and the media are interesting? Give your reasons. • Why is it important to follow the news? • What kind of news do you enjoy reading/hearing about? • Are you more interested in local or international news? If you like, ask students if they, or anyone they know, has been written about in a newspaper . Do they have a class magazine/school newspaper? If so, what kind of articles does it contain and how is it produced? --------------- Coursebook, page 1, Activity 1 Direct students to the six pictures, and discuss with them the different ways of getting news. Ask them to think about how their grandparents got news when they were young. What are the differences between now and then? --------------- Coursebook, page 1, Activity 2 Students read the short text and check the meanings of the words, using dictionaries if necessary. They can work individually or in pairs. T ell students to copy the words and their meanings into their vocabulary or exercise books. Note: The core words for each theme should be given as a spelling test at the end of the theme. The core words for Theme 1 appear in the Glossary in the Review and Reference section on page 16 of the Coursebook. Explain to students that they should learn these words, and that you will be checking them at the end of the theme. journalism: the job of reporting, writing, photographing or broadcasting news choice: something that you have selected transformed: changed gathered: collected from different places demanding: requiring something that you think is necessary social media: websites and other online ways of communication used to share information, such as T witter the Press: printed publications such as newspapers and magazines source: place where something begins headlines: headings of articles in newspapers grab: take suddenly and quickly interviews: formal meetings in which one person asks another person questions celebrities: famous people such as actors, politicians and sports stars Note: Students may ask you the difference between a journalist and a reporter . The two words have similar meanings, although ‘journalist’ is used in a wider sense than ‘reporter’ and covers more aspects of communicating news. --------------- Coursebook, pages 2 and 3 Workbook, pages 2 and 3 Lead-in This unit focuses on press photography, and careers in press photography.

It includes an interview with an Omani press photographer , and also covers the topic of celebrities. Make sure that students understand the 3 Theme 1 Unit 1 Press Photography • Teacher’s Book • meaning of ‘the Press. ’ Refer them to the words in bold in Coursebook, Page 1, Activity 2. They should have checked the meanings of these words already. --------------- Coursebook, page 2, Activity 1 Ask students to discuss the picture in groups. Go round the groups, eliciting feedback as to what the picture shows and why it is effective. The saying in Question b (‘One picture is worth a thousand words’) expresses the idea that one picture can convey something more efficiently and effectively than many words. For example, we can understand how a piece of machinery works much better by looking at pictures rather than reading a description. Note: It is not clear where the saying originated. Some say it was in China or Japan thousands of years ago, but others say that it was first used by an American newspaper editor in 1911. Note: The main purpose of this picture is to show how a dramatic scene can be brought to life visually rather than through words. However , you might also like to use the picture as an opportunity to raise students’ awareness about the dangers of flooded wadis. Water safety in Oman will be fully explored in Theme 3, Unit 3. --------------- Coursebook, page 2, Activity 2 This reading activity gives practice with skimming. Ask students to read the four alternative headings, and guess the meaning of paparazzi . They skim the text as quickly as possible to see if they were right. The correct answer is d . Remind students that the first couple of sentences of a paragraph often give key information about the topic of that paragraph. The answer to the meaning of ‘paparazzi’ is given in the second sentence of the second paragraph of the text (lines 10-11). Note: The correct pronounciation of ‘paparazzi’ is as a three syllable word ‘papa - rat - si’ (phonetic transcription = /pap əˈ ratsi/). --------------- Coursebook, page 3, Activity 3 Students read the text in Activity 2 again. Before they read, ask them to list the six words in the column on the left in their exercise books. As they read, they should find the words in the text and match each word to one of the meanings on the right. Note: T ell students that for this and similar exercises, it is important to write out the words and their meanings in full.

Answers: 1 e 2 a 3 d 4 f 5 c 6 b --------------- Workbook, page 2, Activity 1 In this activity, students read the text in Coursebook, Activity 2 in more detail, and give short answers to questions. They should write the answers into their exercise books. Make sure that students understand they cannot write more than four words for each answer (not all answers will be four words). Answers: 1 Any of the following but not more than four words in total: actors, actresses, singers, sports personalities, politicians 2 photographer (in a film) 3 start false fire alarms 4 the paparazzi 4 Theme 1 Unit 1 Press Photography • Teacher’s Book • and make sure students understand they have to shade in the correct bubble for each item. Answers: 1 newspapers and magazines 2 developing pictures 3 photography 4 want to get news quickly --------------- Coursebook, page 3, Time to Talk This activity encourages students to think more about celebrities and paparazzi. It aims to develop their speaking skills as well as their critical thinking and debating skills. Before students start their group discussions, give them time to make notes individually to answer the questions. They can use the material presented in Activity 2 of the Coursebook to help them, but you should encourage them to use their own ideas as well. After students have had sufficient time to discuss the questions, ask a presenter from each group to summarise the views and ideas of their group, and open the discussion out to the whole class. Additional writing activity: Ask students to write a paragraph summarising their views about paparazzi photographers and the rights of celebrities. Additional speaking activity: Students think of an international or national celebrity, then make notes about that person and tell their group about them. Encourage students to choose a variety of people and not the same person as other members of their group! T ell students to make notes about their person based on the guidelines given, and to work from these notes when they are speaking. Their notes should be written as phrases rather than complete sentences. What would be the advantages and disadvantages of such a career?

chunks.text: Their notes should be written as phrases rather than complete sentences. Workbook, page 2, Activity 2 Discuss with students whether they would be interested in a career in press photography, and to give their reasons. What would be the advantages and disadvantages of such a career? Point out to students that although press photography is a rewarding and creative job with travel and excitement, it is not a job for everyone. Y ou have to be in the right place at the right time to capture good images. The job involves unsocial hours, including evenings and weekends. For example, if you are a sports photographer , you need to be ready to attend sporting events at any time. Y ou have to be able to work under pressure and meet tight deadlines. Students read the text in detail and do the T rue/False/Not Given activity. Repeat as necessary Laila: Good morning. My name’s Laila. I’m doing research for TVC about what people enjoy doing in their leisure time. Can you spare a few minutes to talk to me? Khalid: Well, OK…..if it doesn’t take too long. Laila: Great. First, a few general questions. I take it your age is between 22 and 50? Khalid (laughing) : Y es, that’s right. Somewhere in the middle. Laila: Are you married? Khalid: Y es, I am. I’ve got two boys aged five and three. Laila: And are you in full-time employment? Khalid: Y es, I am. I’m working at the Ministry of Education. Laila: Fine. Now…..let me ask you how you 8 • Teacher’s Book • Theme 1 Unit 2 The Skill of Interviewing spend your leisure time. What do you enjoy doing at weekends? Khalid: Well, my job keeps me very busy, so I don’t have much free time during the week. So at weekends I like visiting family and friends. And I enjoy going to the beach too. Laila: Moving on to the next question…do you have any pets? Khalid: Y es, I have a bird and some small fish. Laila: Do you do any sports? And if so, what sports do you like doing? Khalid: Let me see…..swimming and tennis. Laila: Right. Now let’s talk about TV . How much television do you watch every day? Khalid: Oh, not much at all. Only about half an hour . Laila (laughing) : Oh, so you’re not exactly a TV addict, are you? What kind of programmes do you enjoy most? Khalid: The news, definitely. And sometimes documentaries, if the subject is interesting. Like history, for example. Laila: That’s all. Thank you very much for taking part in this research. Khalid: Y ou’re welcome. Here is some background information about the different areas, and the qualities needed for each one. Background Information Newspaper journalism Many journalists begin their careers as newspaper reporters. Newspaper reporting gives training in basic journalism skills, such as interviewing, writing up stories and working to deadlines. So you need to be good at finding stories and not to mind asking questions, even in difficult circumstances. Magazine journalism There are fewer jobs in magazine journalism than in newspapers.

chunks.text: Newspaper reporting gives training in basic journalism skills, such as interviewing, writing up stories and working to deadlines. So you need to be good at finding stories and not to mind asking questions, even in difficult circumstances. Magazine journalism There are fewer jobs in magazine journalism than in newspapers. Magazines cover a variety of topics such as travel, computers, cars, photography. So you need to specialise in one of them. Magazines tend to have a small staff, so you need to be able to work as part of a close team. TV and radio journalism These branches require the same skills as newspaper journalism, but other skills as well. Y ou need to feel comfortable in front of a camera, and handling a microphone, and tell a story using pictures and sound as well as words. Y ou need to be able to research good stories for TV or radio audiences. Online journalism Y ou don’t need to go out and hunt for stories, but you need an excellent understanding of the web and be able to create special reports on major news themes. Y ou don’t just tell people news; you interact with them and give them the opportunity to express their opinions about it and discuss it with each other . If you’re thinking about a 15 Theme 1 Unit 4 Working in the Media • Teacher’s Book • Listening Script 1.4.2 career in journalism, these are the four most important skills or qualities you need. Firstly, you need to have a passion for giving people news . Y ou need to be very good at communication and give people information that is clear and accurate. Y ou can’t make mistakes! Next, a good journalist needs to be curious . Y ou need to want to learn about everything, and enjoy interviewing people, even in difficult circumstances. Then, you need good writing skills.

chunks.text: Y ou need to be very good at communication and give people information that is clear and accurate. Y ou can’t make mistakes! Next, a good journalist needs to be curious . Y ou need to want to learn about everything, and enjoy interviewing people, even in difficult circumstances. Then, you need good writing skills. Y ou need to write about your stories in a newspaper , or present them on TV , in a coherent way. Y ou need to tell people, ‘This is what happened’ and ‘This is why it is important. ’ Finally, you need to be able to work to deadlines. My job involves choosing people and locations to film, and then organising the filming. (Pause) The thing I enjoy most about the job is meeting people from all walks of life, from tribesmen to pop stars. Every year I find myself filming in places I’ve never heard of, thousands of miles from home. I’m never bored as every trip is different. The biggest challenges are dealing with things when they go wrong. chunks.text: Background Information The Titanic In the 1900s, travel across the Atlantic Ocean from Britain to America was becoming more and more popular . There was a lot of competition among ship companies for customers. In 1907, the White Star Line company decided to build the biggest passenger ship in the world, the Titanic . The Titanic set sail on her first voyage on 10 April 1912 with 2,207 passengers and crew on board. She sailed from Southampton, on the south coast of England, bound for New Y ork. Just before midnight on the evening of 14 April, the Titanic hit a huge iceberg. The iceberg made holes in the ship’s side under the water , and water started flooding in. The ship was sinking. The Captain ordered the crew to prepare the lifeboats. But the problem was that there weren’t enough lifeboats. While the crew began to fill the lifeboats, the radio operators sent messages for help. But the nearest ship, the Carpathia , was four hours away. The Titanic was going to sink in two hours. The Titanic continued to sink, and at last it broke into two pieces. Many people jumped into the sea, hoping to swim to a lifeboat. But the water was freezing cold. By the time the Carpathia arrived, many people had died from the cold or drowned. The Carpathia picked up the survivors and took them to New Y ork. They counted just over 700 survivors, which meant that more than 1,500 of the Titanic ’s passengers and crew had died. The Titanic sank in a very deep part of the Atlantic Ocean. Many people tried to find the ship, but it was not until 1985 that a team of scientists succeeded. In 1987 another team brought many things up from the Titanic . But the ship itself still lies at the bottom of the ocean. --------------- Coursebook, page 10, Activity 1 Questions a has open answers. In answer to question b , the Titanic was such a dramatic news story because the Titanic was the biggest passenger ship in the world, and everyone thought that she was very safe. She was called ‘the unsinkable ship. ’ Note: ‘Titanic’ seemed a good name for the ship because it means something that is very big, strong and impressive. The White Star Line, the company that owned the Titanic , were planning to build two sister ships, the Olympic and the Gigantic . These names tell us that these ships were also going to be huge. Of course, after what happened to the Titanic , the plans for these ships were abandoned. Note: Ships and boats are traditionally feminine in English so we use the pronouns ‘she’ and ‘her’ when referring to them. --------------- 20 • Teacher’s Book • • A T errible Night • A T ragic V oyage Main sentences: The Titanic set sail from Southampton in England on 10 April 1912. Example of Model Story Rescue at Sea One afternoon, Ahmed and his friend, Salim, were fishing in a small boat. The sea was calm and peaceful. At last, they decided to go home. However , when they tried to start the engine, it wouldn’t work. They tried again and again, but it was no good. “It’s broken, ” said Salim. “What shall we do?” “I don’t know, ” replied Ahmed, “but I think there’s going to be a storm. Look at those clouds over the mountains. ” The boat began to drift out to sea. By this time, the waves were getting bigger and the wind was getting stronger . It began to rain. The boys were worried and afraid. Fortunately, a police boat was nearby. One of the policemen saw the boys through his binoculars. “Look!” he said. “That boat’s in trouble. We have to go and help. ” The police boat drove quickly to the boys’ boat, and the police threw the boys a strong rope. Ahmed and Salim were very happy they were safe again. 165 words

In groups, students read the letter and decide what advice they would give to the writer . Give students time to discuss their ideas, then go round the groups and ask a presenter from each group to give feedback to the class. Students may find this activity difficult, so help groups with advice if necessary. Some suggestions for the writer of the letter are: • find out more about the careers she mentions in the letter and to consider whether she has the right personality • make a list of the advantages and disadvantages (pros and cons) of each career – for example, acting is insecure • make a list of the desirable qualifications of each career – for example, it would be good to have a knowledge of languages to be a tour guide Remind students of the phrases used to express suggestions and give advice. Write some examples on the board, such as: • This student should . . . • We think the student should . . . • It would be a good idea for the student to . . . • Why doesn’t the student . . .? • The student needs to . . . Y ou should appear keen and enthusiastic about the job you’re applying for . Advice – Never talk about holidays or ways that you can save yourself work. The interviewer will think that you are lazy and self-centred, with little interest in the job. Ask students what kind of accidents occur in the home (falling from a height, burning, scalding, drowning) and what potential hazards there are in the home (stairs, chemicals, medicines, cookers, electrical sockets, open windows). Ask them which room in the home is the source of most accidents (the kitchen). Background information Accidents in the Home Accidents in and around the home are one of the leading causes of serious injury and death, particularly in young children under five and elderly people over the age of 75. Most of these accidents are preventable. The most common cause of accidents is falling, for example, babies can easily roll off a table, or an elderly person can trip and fall down the stairs. Y oung children are especially at risk because they don’t know if something is dangerous or not. Their lack of experience and development, such as poor co-ordination and balance, can result in injuries. It can sometimes be difficult for parents to realise what their young child is able to do. Babies between 6 and 12 months can stand, sit, crawl and put things in their mouths. As they get older , they’re able to walk and move about, reach things higher up, climb and find hidden objects.

chunks.text: It can sometimes be difficult for parents to realise what their young child is able to do. Babies between 6 and 12 months can stand, sit, crawl and put things in their mouths. As they get older , they’re able to walk and move about, reach things higher up, climb and find hidden objects. Most serious accidents that involve young children are caused by: • falls from a height • burns from fire or hot surfaces • scalds from hot water or other liquids • choking or suffocating • cutting with glass or a sharp object • poisoning • drowning There are potential hazards in every home, such as stairs, chemicals, medicines, cookers, electrical sockets, glass, knives and open windows. Source: www.nhs.uk --------------- Coursebook, page 36, Activity 1 Students look at the pictures and discuss questions a and b . Make sure that students understand the meaning of ‘potential’ and ‘hazard. ’ potential (adj): has the possibility of developing in a particular way hazard (n): A danger or risk; anything which could cause harm Answers: Picture A Potential hazard: The toddler could easily get electrocuted. Prevention: Children should not be allowed to play with electrical equipment. Picture B Potential hazard: Children can swallow medicines and get poisoned. Prevention: Medicines should be locked away out of reach of children, preferably in a safe cabinet or cupboard. Picture C Potential hazard: The young girl is about to pull the pan onto herself and get burned or scalded. Prevention: The pan handle should be turned inwards on the cooker so it is out of reach. Picture D Potential hazard: Children could cut themselves 56 Theme 3 Unit 2 Safety in and around the Home • Teacher’s Book • with these sharp knives. Prevention: Knives should be kept in a safe place out of reach of children. Picture E Potential hazard: The barbecue has caught fire which is in danger of spreading. Prevention: The barbecue should not be left without anyone to supervise it. Picture F Potential hazard: The woman could trip on the toy on the stairs and fall. Prevention: The stairs should be kept clear of objects that people could fall over . --------------- Coursebook, page 36, Activity 2 Students complete the gap fill activity using the verbs in the box. In question a , ask students if they can guess the meaning of the phrase ‘prone to. ’ Prone to: likely to have or be affected by something. ‘Prone to’ can be followed by either a noun or a verb. Write some example sentences on the board, such as: • The coastal region is prone to heavy flooding. • She is prone to losing her keys. • Since he was a boy, he has been prone to headaches. Ask students to make up some sentences of their own using ‘prone to’. Write the best ones on the board. Give students a few minutes to discuss the three questions, then go round the groups, eliciting feedback. If you like, open the discussion out into a class discussion. For question b , here are some suggestions about how to prepare for a flood (but students may be able to think of other ways): • check for flood warnings on the local radio • alert your neighbours, particularly elderly people and people who have just moved into the area • prepare an emergency kit with items such as a first aid box, a torch, water and medicines • pack essential items such as warm clothes to take with you in case you have to evacuate your home • if possible, move cars to higher ground • if you have to evacuate your home, shut windows, lock doors and turn off gas and electricity and water supplies Ways of how to prepare for a cyclone are similar . Additional suggestions are: • remain indoors until you are advised it is safe to go out • stay in the strongest part of the house and keep away from windows • close shutters, board up windows and lock doors • prepare a stock of candles, a torch, medicines, food and water • if caught in the cyclone when you are driving, keep away from the sea and trees Note: Students may be able to talk about cyclones from personal experience if they or relatives or friends were caught in Cyclone Gonu which hit Oman in 2007, or Cyclone Phet which happened in 2010. --------------- Coursebook, page 38, Activity 2 Students read through the list of natural disasters and check the meanings in their dictionaries.

As they listen, they have to complete the missing words in a summary of the talk. Make sure they understand that the text in the Workbook is not an exact transcript of the talk – it is a summary. Before students listen, tell them to read the summary carefully in order to get the sense of it. Get them to try and predict what word should go into each gap. Point out that the missing word has to make sense in meaning, and also be grammatically correct. For example, for the first word, students should be able to predict important . Elicit students' suggestions and write them on the board. Play Listening 3.3.1 . Repeat as necessary. The answers are at the end of the listening script. Good afternoon. T oday I’m going to talk about a topic of growing concern in Oman – water safety. Every year , people die from accidents in the water , and many of these are children. Therefore, it’s important for children learn to swim from an early age. An accident can happen in just seconds and it takes only minutes to drown. If children can swim, it can save their lives. In Oman, there are three main areas where water-related accidents happen – in the sea, in swimming pools and in wadis. All these places can be very dangerous for children. However , schools can help educate children about water safety, and swimming lessons should be part of the school curriculum. If you’re at a swimming pool, you should always pay attention to the lifeguard and follow his 62 • Teacher’s Book • Theme 3 Unit 3 Be Prepared! instructions. People often get into trouble because they don’t realise that the swimming pool is not the same depth all over , and slopes quickly from shallow to deep water . When you’re out and about in Oman, either at the beach or in the wadis, you should keep a close eye on weather conditions because they can change very rapidly. Keep alert at all times, and if you see storm clouds gathering, be very careful. If there is a sudden downpour , it can cause flash floods. Most importantly, never attempt to cross a wadi which is overflowing after heavy rain. It is important that students do not confuse facts and opinions. Note: We use facts to explain or instruct, for example, when describing how something is made or produced, or how to use a new camera. We use opinions to present an argument, for example, that we need to raise awareness about water safety. We use facts (evidence and examples) to support our opinion and make our argument stronger , for example, statistics to show the rise in deaths from drowning in the sea or wadis. Point out that opinions are often introduced by phrases with verbs such as think , feel or believe . These can often be found in the negative – e.g. don’t think . --------------- Coursebook, page 43, Activity 4 Students read the six statements and decide if they are facts or opinions. In Activity 3, they make notes to support their ideas. Direct students to the example in Column B, which gives three reasons why garbage should be put in litter bins. These reasons show how the idea (of putting garbage in litter bins) can be made stronger by giving evidence and details. --------------- Workbook, page 39, Activity 4 This activity gives practice with ways of expressing opinions. Direct students back to Activity 2, and tell them to use the notes they made in Columns A and B to write three sentences expressing their opinions, using a different opinion phrase to introduce each sentence. One of their sentences should start with a negative opinion phrase. Go round the class, eliciting sentences, and write some examples on the board. --------------- Workbook, page 39, Activity 5 Students write an evaluative essay about the best ways to improve road safety in Oman. T ell them to follow the method outlined for the essay about keeping Oman clean and healthy in Activities 2, 3 and 4 of this unit. Refer them to the Writing Guide on pages 82-83 of their Workbook for help with layout and language. If students are having difficulty thinking of ideas to improve road safety, here are some ideas you can suggest: • more speed cameras • more speed bumps in residential areas Answers: a 5 (the first five sentences) b 2 (the last two sentences) c in my view (in the sixth sentence) I believe (in the seventh sentence) --------------- Workbook, page 38, Activity 2 Remind students that it is very important to plan what information they are going to include in an essay before they start writing. It will help them greatly to have a plan to follow when writing, as this will give their essay a clear and logical structure. T ell students to work in groups. Their task is to consider the title of the essay in Activity 1, ‘The Best Ways to Make Oman Clean and Healthy’ and to write their ideas about what should be included in the essay into the circles. If they have more than six ideas, tell them to add more circles. Give students time to discuss their ideas, then go round the groups, eliciting feedback, and write the best ideas on the board.

chunks.text: Their task is to consider the title of the essay in Activity 1, ‘The Best Ways to Make Oman Clean and Healthy’ and to write their ideas about what should be included in the essay into the circles. If they have more than six ideas, tell them to add more circles. Give students time to discuss their ideas, then go round the groups, eliciting feedback, and write the best ideas on the board. Ideas that students might come up (although they will probably have other ideas too): • organise anti-littering media campaigns • raise awareness in schools about why throwing litter is bad • encourage people to think of their country as their home (you keep your home clean and healthy) • reduce the number of plastic bags • make people pay for plastic bags in supermarkets rather than getting them for free • use recycled materials • organise regular clean-ups of beaches and other beauty spots • bring in strict anti-littering laws • enforce the laws with heavy fines, and community service for people who throw litter 70 Theme 3 Unit 5 What Do Y ou Think? • Teacher’s Book • • more police patrol cars on the roads • heavier fines and/or jail sentences for drivers who speed or ‘jump’ red lights • raising road safety awareness, especially among young people • laws to improve child safety in cars • stricter laws against behaviour which leads to accidents, such as using mobile phones while driving, ‘tail gating’ other drivers and not wearing seatbelts • better training for driving instructors Example of an Evaluative Essay The Best Ways to Improve Road Safety in Oman Although the number of road accidents in Oman has decreased in recent years, I believe that there are several things we can do to make our roads safer . In my view, there should be stricter laws to improve child safety in cars. We often see small children without seatbelts. This is extremely dangerous because it is very distracting for the driver and can lead to accidents. I think that training for driving instructors should be better as they lack qualifications and experience in teaching. T o be a driving instructor , you need to be Omani, to have had a driving licence for five years, to be fit and be able to read and write. However , this is not enough to be able to teach someone to drive well. Speed cameras are effective but I don’t believe that installing more cameras alone will help to improve road safety. We need to introduce other measures too. For example, putting in more speed bumps in residential areas will help to slow traffic down and reduce accidents. In conclusion, I believe that all the ways mentioned above would be effective in improving road safety in Oman.

chunks.text: 74 Theme 4 Unit 1 Being a Citizen • Teacher’s Book • Lead-in Ask students if they know what the word citizenship means. Citizenship is the status of being a citizen. Citizens have the right to live, work and vote in a country. Background Information This unit is about citizenship. According to the Citizenship Foundation, key elements of citizenship education include: Knowledge and understanding : About topics such as: laws and rules, the democratic process, the media, human rights, diversity, money and the economy, sustainable development and the world as a global community; and about concepts such as democracy, justice, equality, freedom, authority and the rule of law. Skills and aptitudes : Critical thinking, analysing information, expressing opinions, taking part in discussions and debates, negotiating, conflict resolution and participating in community action. Values and dispositions : Respect for justice, democracy and the rule of law, openness, tolerance, courage to defend a point of view and a willingness to listen to, work with and stand up for others. You can find more information here: http://www.citizenshipfoundation.org.uk/ --------------- Coursebook, page 49, Activity 1 Direct students to the five photos and the title of the theme. Ask them to discuss in groups what they think the theme is about and what topics might come up. Elicit feedback from the class. --------------- Coursebook, page 49, Activity 2 Students read the short text and check the meanings of the words in bold, using a dictionary if necessary. They can work individually or in pairs. All the words will occur somewhere within the theme. Tell students to copy the words and their meanings into their vocabulary or exercise books. Note : The core words for each theme should be given as a spelling test at the end of the theme. The core words for Theme 4 appear in the Glossary in the Review and Reference section on page 64 of the Coursebook. Explain to students that they should learn these words and that you will be checking them at the end of the theme.

chunks.text: Note : The core words for each theme should be given as a spelling test at the end of the theme. The core words for Theme 4 appear in the Glossary in the Review and Reference section on page 64 of the Coursebook. Explain to students that they should learn these words and that you will be checking them at the end of the theme. citizen: someone who has the legal right to live in a particular country right: something you are legally or morally allowed to do or have vote: to choose someone or something through an election legal responsibilities: something that must be done for legal reasons law: an official rule that people must obey ethical responsibilities: something that must be done for ethical reasons Civil Participation: improving the quality of life in a community through political and non- political processes NGO: non-governmental organisation that works to improve a particular issue participate: to take part in something community: a group of people who live together in the same place global: including or affecting the whole world Coursebook, pages 50 and 51 Workbook, pages 44 and 45 Lead-in Ask students to think about the title of this unit. Ask them what different things might be involved in being a citizen. Students discuss in groups. Then elicit feedback from the whole class and write their ideas on the board. 75 Theme 4 Unit 1 Being a Citizen • Teacher’s Book • Coursebook, page 51, Activity 4 This activity focuses on vocabulary development. Students match words with their meanings. First ask students to try and guess the meanings of the words from the context of the text in Activity 2. After doing the matching exercise, they should check the meanings in their dictionaries. Answers: e 1 a 2 f 3 b 4 d 5 c 6 --------------- Coursebook, page 51, Activity 5 Students look at the pairs of words and decide if their meanings are similar (S) or different (D). Ask students to compare their answers in pairs. Then elicit feedback. --------------- Answers: S 1 D 2 S 3 D 4 S 5 S 6 --------------- Workbook, page 44, Activity 1 Note: Schools in Oman have been sent a copy of Dr Nemer’s book Citizenship Education in the Thinking of Sultan Qaboos. You may be able to find a copy in your Learning Resource Centre. Show students a copy of Dr Nemer’s book, or ask them to look at the picture of it in the Workbook. Coursebook, page 50, Activity 1 Students work with a partner and discuss the three questions. Give them time to discuss the questions, then go round the group and elicit feedback. --------------- Coursebook, page 50, Activity 2 Students scan the text about citizenship to find the answers to the three questions in Activity 1.

chunks.text: Coursebook, page 50, Activity 1 Students work with a partner and discuss the three questions. Give them time to discuss the questions, then go round the group and elicit feedback. --------------- Coursebook, page 50, Activity 2 Students scan the text about citizenship to find the answers to the three questions in Activity 1. Answers: A person can be a citizen if they were 1 born in a country or if they move to a country and are granted citizenship by legal process. The concept of citizenship has extended 2 beyond a person’s country. A person may be a citizen of a regional area e.g. the GCC, or even a global or world citizen. --------------- Coursebook, page 51, Activity 3 This activity focuses on reading the text in more detail to find specific information. Students re-read the text in Activity 2 and write answers to the three questions. Check the answers together. Answers: The right to live in a country and the right 1 to participate in political process. Any two of the following answers: 2 paying taxes - obeying the law - serving in the military - 3 Any two of the following answers: respecting the rights of others - making an effort to improve local - communities being informed about and actively - involved in Civil Participation protecting common resources such as - the environment. 76 Theme 4 Unit 1 Being a Citizen • Teacher’s Book • Workbook, page 45, Activity 4 Explain that the suffix –ship forms nouns. Ask students to read the information about the four basic meanings of words with –ship. Students complete the gap fill using words with –ship. There are two extra answer choices. Elicit feedback from the class. Answers: relationship 1 leadership 2 championship 3 scholarship 4 citizenship 5 sponsorship 6 --------------- Workbook, page 45, Activity 5 Note: Role plays are a useful citizenship education tool. Acting out different scenarios can raise awareness of issues related to citizenship and help develop good values and attitudes. Organise students into pairs. One student is ‘Student A’. The other is ‘Student B’. Students read the scenarios and then role play the situations. Remind students that some of the new vocabulary from this unit might be useful for their role plays. Choose pairs to perform their role plays for the class. --------------- Coursebook, page 51, Time to Talk The aim of this activity is to personalise the information in the text and help students be more aware of their actions and responsibilities as Omani citizens. Students work in pairs to think of two questions they would like to ask Dr Nemer about his book. Elicit some questions from students and write them on the board. --------------- Workbook, page 44, Activity 2 Students read the interview with Dr Nemer.

chunks.text: --------------- Coursebook, page 51, Time to Talk The aim of this activity is to personalise the information in the text and help students be more aware of their actions and responsibilities as Omani citizens. Students work in pairs to think of two questions they would like to ask Dr Nemer about his book. Elicit some questions from students and write them on the board. --------------- Workbook, page 44, Activity 2 Students read the interview with Dr Nemer. As they read, they should see if they can find answers to their questions from Activity 1 in the text. After reading, go through the questions on the board from Activity 1 and elicit any answers that students found in the text. --------------- Workbook, page 45, Activity 3 Students re-read the text and answer the four questions. Ask students to check their answers in pairs. Then elicit feedback. Answers: Dr Nemer found that Sultan Qaboos 1 often talked about elements of citizenship in his speeches, even if the speeches were not directly about citizenship. Citizenship education is integrated into 2 the curriculum. But there are also specific projects to develop citizenship skills and values, such as For the sake of my country. Dr Nemer's definition includes the 3 concept of 'emotional attachment' to your country, people and history. This was not mentioned in the Coursebook text. Additional discussion activity: Ask students to think of any examples of citizenship education in their own school. Examples might include projects like the one mentioned by Dr Nemer in the interview, or events such as National Day celebrations. Elicit any ideas students have. 77 Theme 4 Unit 2 NGOs • Teacher’s Book • Students think of three ways in which they feel they are a responsible citizen. Remind them to refer to the text from Activity 2 for ideas about being a responsible citizen. Students then share their ideas in groups. Each group should decide who the most responsible citizen in their group is. Go around the groups, ask them to name their most responsible citizen and explain why they selected that student. To extend the activity, you could have a class vote to choose the most responsible citizen in the class from those students nominated by their groups. Coursebook, pages 52 and 53 Workbook, pages 46 and 47 Note: NGO stands for non-governmental organisation. NGOs are non-profit, non- governmental, non-political, non-business organisations. They are generally concerned with improving a particular issue and often rely on donations and voluntary service. Students should be familiar with the term NGO from the unit overview on page 49 of the Coursebook. Lead-in Ask students to look at the title of the unit and discuss how NGOs relate to the theme of Citizenship.

Doing good is considered one of the main Islamic principles. Islam urges every Muslim to do good in this life, to serve their society voluntarily by helping the weak, educating the ignorant, guiding the lost, aiding the disabled, and helping the needy who appeal for help. It is peaceful and hospitable. Omani people are very friendly and welcoming, and they are very proud of their country. It’s a very family orientated society, and that’s important to me. It’s not the same in the UK. I also love having an outdoor life. Oman’s nature is very diverse. You can spend your weekends on the sea, at the beach, hiking in wadis or in the mountains, or you can go into the desert. Interviewer: What do you think your responsibilities as an Omani citizen are? Elayne: Oman has very strong moral and cultural values, and I think it’s my responsibility as a citizen to uphold these values. I’m a marine biologist and I’m really passionate about Oman’s marine life. I want to contribute to Oman by helping educate people about the marine life here.

chunks.text: Elayne: Oman has very strong moral and cultural values, and I think it’s my responsibility as a citizen to uphold these values. I’m a marine biologist and I’m really passionate about Oman’s marine life. I want to contribute to Oman by helping educate people about the marine life here. I also want to preserve it because it can be so easily damaged through overfishing and development, especially with all the new hotels being built along the coast. I feel it’s my duty to spread awareness about an issue that I’m passionate about. Interviewer: In what ways are you similar or different to an Omani who was born in Oman? Elayne: I’m similar to Omanis who were born in Oman because I’m very proud of the country and what it has achieved and how it sets an example in the Middle East. I’m different because I don’t dress like an Omani on a daily basis, or eat Omani food on a daily basis and I can’t speak Arabic fluently, although I hope to improve my Arabic. Also, I would never drop litter from my car because it is really bad for the environment. Interviewer: What three words would you choose to describe Omanis? Elayne: Omanis are hospitable, proud and generous. Interviewer: Thank you very much, Elayne. It was lovely to meet you. Elayne: Thank you. --------------- Coursebook, page 56, Activity 3 In this activity, students practise listening for specific details and taking notes as they listen. Ask students what they think about globalisation. Do they think it is a positive or negative thing? Do they think it has affected life in Oman? How? In this unit students write an informative essay. The activities in the Coursebook and Workbook all lead up to this task. This unit is about global citizenship. According to Oxfam, a global citizen is someone who: Is aware of the wider world and has a • sense of their role as a world citizen. Respects and values diversity. • Has an understanding of how the world • works. Is passionately committed to social • justice. Participates in the community at a • range of levels, from the local to the global. Works with others to make the world • a more equitable and sustainable place. Takes responsibility for their actions. • You can find more information here: http://www.oxfam.org.uk/education/global- citizenship --------------- Coursebook, page 58, Activity 1 The purpose of this activity is to activate students’ knowledge about the topic of this unit ‘global citizenship’. Draw the table on the board. Elicit feedback and write students’ ideas into the table. Issues that are important to them include the environment, poverty, trade, health, peace and human rights. Why? We need to find ways to provide food, water and energy to over 7 billion people as natural resources become fewer and fewer. It is essential for people from different countries to work together.

Explain that cohesion can be created by moving from general to specific information and by writing paragraphs with one clear topic. Cohesion can also be created using a range of cohesive devices, such as repetition of key words, conjunctions ( and, but, moreover ), and pronouns ( it, they, this, that ) to link back to nouns. 89 • Teacher’s Book • Workbook, page 53, Activity 3 Direct students to the phrase in the second paragraph of the essay ‘The focus on cultural and religious tolerance in Oman….” Explain that this phrase has been replaced with the phrase “ This attitude”. The use of the pronoun this helps create cohesion because it refers backwards to the information in the previous sentence. Using the word attitude avoids repetition of the same information. Too much repetition makes an essay difficult to read. 3.1 Ask students to locate the other three phrases in the essay that have been underlined. Students replace these phrases with this or these and the words provided in the box. Answers: This attitude 1 This policy 2 These relationships 3 These talks 4 3.2 Students underline any other words or phrases in the essay that help to link sentences together. Check the answers with students. Answers: In addition (line 4) At a local level (line 6) This means that (line 9) At a global level (line 10) As a result (line 13) One reason (line 18) Another reason (line 19) --------------- Workbook, page 53, Activity 4 This activity prepares students to write an informative essay explaining how their classmates can be better global citizens in one of the following areas: environment, poverty, trade, health or peace. Students brainstorm what their chosen topic is about, how their classmates can be better global citizens in this area and why it is important to be active or contribute in their chosen area. Some examples have been given in the area of environment to give students some ideas. Below is an example of an informative essay about global citizenship and the environment. Our role as global citizens in protecting the environment Global citizens consider themselves members of global communities as well as citizens of their own country. One issue that is important to global citizens is the environment. This essay outlines what contributing to the environment as a global citizen involves, how local students can contribute and why this is important. What does contributing to the environment as a global citizen involve? Protecting the environment involves different activities such as developing environmentally friendly habits, raising awareness about issues and participating in events. Students can easily get involved in activities like these to be more active in protecting the environment. How can local students help improve the environment? One of the simplest things students can do to protect the environment is to always put litter in a bin. Dropping litter is a serious problem in Oman which spoils many beautiful places. Many animals and fish die because they eat discarded plastic. If everyone stopped this harmful habit, the environment of Oman would be instantly improved. Students can also join environmental organisations, such as ESO and volunteer at events such as beach clean-ups. Why is protecting the environment important? It is important we protect the environment so that future generations will have sufficient resources and a healthy environment to live in. Small changes at a local level can result in big benefits for the environment. The Course The Coursebooks for Grades 11 and 12 of the Engage With English course were originally designed to reflect the more mature status of students of this age, and to maintain motivation and interest. In 2011, the original materials in Grade 11 were revised and updated in response to feedback and suggestions offered by teachers and students in schools throughout Oman. This was followed by revision of the Grade 12 materials in 2015. The new course materials cover a wide range of topics. Every attempt has been made to include material likely to be of special relevance and interest to students – for example, Those Teenage Things (Grade 11A, Theme 2) and Starting University (Grade 12A, Theme 2). 1.1 Course Structure At the request of teachers, the number of themes in each of the Grade 11 and 12 books has been reduced from five to four. This allows the course to be completed at a more comfortable pace, and particularly for teachers to be able to devote more time to writing activities in class. Each theme consists of five two-page units, each of which focuses on a specific language and skills area. This format gives coherence to the overall theme, but also allows for a greater variety of topics and vocabulary to be introduced.

chunks.title: دليل المعلم مادة اللغة الإنجليزية teachers book للصف الثاني عشر الفصل الأول
chunks.text: This allows the course to be completed at a more comfortable pace, and particularly for teachers to be able to devote more time to writing activities in class. Each theme consists of five two-page units, each of which focuses on a specific language and skills area. This format gives coherence to the overall theme, but also allows for a greater variety of topics and vocabulary to be introduced. 1.2 Course Aims The general aims of the course are to raise students’ language level to a good general standard so that they are prepared to enter the career area they have chosen and develop their specific language skills further. The curriculum design is meant to serve the needs of all Omani students during their last years of secondary education, not just those going on to further education. The overall aims of the English Language Curriculum for Grades 11 and 12 are as follows: 1.To provide students with a functional command of English as preparation for work or further studies 2.To develop and consolidate functional skills in English. 3.To give students the skills and confidence to use English outside the classroom. 4.To develop students’ awareness of learning strategies they can apply to further their learning of English both inside and outside school. 5.To enable students to acquire active mastery of the core grammar of English. 6.To establish a basis for both fluency and accuracy within specified domains. 7.To use English as a medium for learning about other cultures and contrasting it with their own. In addition to the linguistic aims, there are also a range of non-linguistic objectives embedded in the course. Learning Strategies Lifelong, independent learning strategies are an important objective of the curriculum. The course materials provide opportunities for students to become familiar with self-help strategies, the appropriate use of a range of resources for independent learning and reflection and monitoring strategies. Study Skills Study skills are a key feature of the curriculum to help students to become more self-directed. Basic study skills such as dictionary skills, library and research skills, paraphrasing, referencing and accurate citation of sources are built into the class materials in Grades 11 and 12. Culture English is presented as an international language that provides a means of communicating with other users of English both inside and outside Oman. xiii • Teacher’s Book • Introduction International Perspectives The themes and topics of the course provide an international outlook and cover a range of issues which have a global impact. Students will be encouraged to reflect on these issues and relate the subject matter and its implications to their own, specifically Omani experience.

chunks.title: دليل المعلم مادة اللغة الإنجليزية teachers book للصف الثاني عشر الفصل الأول
chunks.text: xiii • Teacher’s Book • Introduction International Perspectives The themes and topics of the course provide an international outlook and cover a range of issues which have a global impact. Students will be encouraged to reflect on these issues and relate the subject matter and its implications to their own, specifically Omani experience. Vocational A number of themes link either directly or indirectly to the various vocational fields that many of the students will be entering. An example of this is the tourism and hospitality industry. Many of the language functions that are reviewed or newly introduced are transferable across several vocational fields. Cross-Curricular Links Many of the themes are linked to other subject areas of the curriculum, such as the Social Sciences. Language and concepts introduced in one subject are recycled, reviewed and extended in other subject areas. A summary of the cross-curricular links is given on pages vi – ix of this Teacher’s Book. Learner Training During the course, teachers should encourage students to use strategies which will help them become more independent and self-directed. Students will learn general planning and organisational skills, and self-monitoring skills. For example, they will continue to be encouraged to plan, draft, check and re-draft pieces of writing until they are satisfied with a final draft. Methodology The curriculum is based on a communicative and skills-based methodology which encourages active student participation and collaboration, rather than a teacher-fronted and dominated classroom methodology. The teaching methodology contains the following characteristics: 1.There is a consistent focus on learning English in order to develop practical and functional skills, rather than as an end in itself. 2.Students are involved in practical activities which relate to real-world use of English. 3. Realistic and communicative use of language is given priority. 4.Maximum opportunities for student-student interaction are provided. 5.Maximum use is made of pair and group activities where students undertake tasks collaboratively. 6.There is a balance between accuracy-based and fluency-based activities. 7.The course materials contain less teacher-centred teaching and more learner-directed activities. Teachers are expected to act as facilitators of learning rather than as presenters of information. 1.3 Overview of course materials 1.3.1 The Coursebook The Coursebook is divided into four themes, which are each divided into five units. Each unit focuses on one particular language skill – Reading (Unit 1), Grammar (Unit 2), Vocabulary (Unit 3), Listening and Speaking (Unit 4), and Writing (Unit 5).

chunks.text: 1.3 Overview of course materials 1.3.1 The Coursebook The Coursebook is divided into four themes, which are each divided into five units. Each unit focuses on one particular language skill – Reading (Unit 1), Grammar (Unit 2), Vocabulary (Unit 3), Listening and Speaking (Unit 4), and Writing (Unit 5). However, this main skill is not practised in isolation, as the activities are designed to relate it to other skills. At the end of each theme, there are two two-page spreads entitled Across Cultures and Reading for Pleasure. These are designed as ‘stand-alone’ units which can either be used in class, or if the teacher prefers, allocated for self-study at home. There is a Review and Reference page at the end of each theme which summarises the skills which have been covered, and lists a glossary of 12 – 14 key words introduced in the theme. Communication activity and role play materials are also provided at the back of the Coursebook. It is very important for teachers to tell students not to write in the Coursebook. All written work is to be done in the Workbook, or in students’ exercise books. From time to time, for example after the Time to Talk activities, students are given the task of writing paragraphs based on the ideas generated by their group discussions. The first xiv • Teacher’s Book • Introduction drafts of these paragraphs should be done in class, so that the teacher can monitor students and offer guidance. Students should edit their work, and produce a second or final draft at home. They should attach their final drafts to previous drafts, and put everything into their portfolios. This ensures that a record is kept of the stages which led to the final version produced by students. 1.3.2 The Workbook The format of the Workbook mirrors that of the Coursebook. The Workbook provides practice and consolidation activities for each of the five skills-based units within the theme. At the end of each theme, there is a page of Across Cultures activities which can be done in class or as self-study activities. An answer key is provided both in the Workbook and the Teacher’s Book. There is also one page of Reading for Pleasure , which is related to the Reading for Pleasure material in the Coursebook. There are two Review and Reference pages at the end of each theme which provide revision activities for the grammar introduced in that theme, as well as a vocabulary activity based on the words and phrases in the Glossary at the end of each theme in the Coursebook.

chunks.text: There is also one page of Reading for Pleasure , which is related to the Reading for Pleasure material in the Coursebook. There are two Review and Reference pages at the end of each theme which provide revision activities for the grammar introduced in that theme, as well as a vocabulary activity based on the words and phrases in the Glossary at the end of each theme in the Coursebook. The end material of the Workbook in Grade 12 consists of: • a Reading Section with comprehension questions for timed reading practice • Communication Activities • Grammar Practice Activities • a Writing Guide Section for each theme • a Grammar Reference Section for each theme • a Word List for each theme • a Functional Language Review for each theme • Answers to the Across Cultures and Review and Reference activities. The Grammar Practice activities are a new feature of the Grade 11 and 12 Workbooks, and provide students with further opportunities to practise the grammar presented in Unit 2 of each theme. 1.3.3 The Teacher’s Book The Teacher’s Book provides an introduction to the curriculum for Grades 11 and 12, an outline of the course components and detailed suggestions about how to use the course materials. Listening scripts are provided throughout the teaching notes. 1.3.4 Course CD All recordings used during the course are included on a CD supplied with the other course components. 2. Course Materials 2.1 The Coursebook The Coursebook opens with a Contents Map, which outlines the syllabus. This is followed by a two-page spread with the learning objectives for each theme, for students’ easy reference. 2.1.1 Overview page The overview page for each theme is intended to introduce the topic, and activate students’ prior knowledge about the subject. Students are usually asked to look at a number of photographs or pictures and discuss their content and/or some questions associated with the general theme. There is also a short text that introduces the sub-themes and which contains relevant vocabulary. A number of words and phrases are presented in bold lettering, all of which will occur in the theme. These words can be used for spelling practice, in addition to the 12 – 14 words presented in the Glossary in the Review and Reference section at the end of each theme in the Coursebook. 2.1.2 Reading The focus of Unit 1 in each theme is reading. Students read a variety of reading texts using a range of strategies and reading skills. The materials in this unit focus on different reading micro-skills, such as ‘recognising topic sentences’ or ‘inferring information’. Realistic purposes for reading are developed with naturalistic texts being used in a variety of text types. Both informational reading and reading for
